newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: El Nino not to peak until December - scientists.
newsitem.headline: El Nino not to peak until December - scientists.

text.p: The El Nino weather pattern developing in the tropical Pacific Ocean is unlikely to peak until December 1997 and should persist for months afterwards, weather experts said on Friday.

An El Nino pattern is forming, possibly rivalling in severity one in 1982/83 that caused widespread droughts, flooding and fires in many parts of the world, scientists meeting in Melbourne for an international conference on weather said.

"In terms of the warming of the water and the southern oscillation index, it is on a par with the 1982/83 pattern," Tom Spence, head of the climate observing system for the World Meteorological Organisation said.
The southern oscillation index is a measure of the difference in air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia. A low index means drought.

In Australia during that period, damage to crops and livestock was estimated at around A$2 billion and reduced overall GDP by two percent. In Ecuador, flooding during the period caused an estimated US$640 million in damages.
"What we're saying is that in 1997, El Nino has already signed on," Mary Voice, head of climate analysis for Australia's Bureau of Meteorology said.

The scientists urged farmers and others in rural areas to assess their risks from the effects of El Nino, possibly making changes to plantings patterns and crops in anticipation of severe farming conditions.
"We expect this system has taken on a momentum that will play out over about the next year," Roger Lukas a weather specialist from the University of Hawaii, said.
El Nino typically brings drought to parts of Australia, while causing monsoon-like rains in regions of South America.
Rainfall in southern Australia was well below average consistent with characteristics of an El Nino, the Australia's Bureau of Meteorology warned this week.
Abnormally dry conditions are already evident in parts of southeastern Australia, while Ecuador and Chile have been hit by heavy rains.

"We are now able to observe the magnitude of the warming of the Pacific Ocean and how its progressed over several months," William Kininmonth, superintendent of the Australian Bureau of Meteorology's National Climate Centre.
"The magnitude of the warming means it will take several months to dissipate and meanwhile we're still on a warming trend,"
Simulation modelling of the pattern further indicated the peak would not occur until December.

Additional rainfall was forecast to occur in some parts of South America, including southern Brazil and Argentina as moisture is drawn southward in the Pacific across South America and feeds into the local weather systems, Kininmonth said.
Central Africa should see abnormally high rains, as well, Kininmonth said.
